summary: Describes a model for managing virtual terminals, which lets different kinds of terminals and workstations talk to remote systems in a common way. It was prepared for the Defense Communications Agency by MITRE.

plainLanguage.summary: Different screens and keyboards all behave a little differently. This report imagines a pretend standard terminal so any real one can be translated to it.

subtitle: An architectural model for managing different kinds of terminals in a unified way.

tldr.problem: Different terminals and workstations have different keyboards, displays, and capabilities. When a workstation needs to talk to a remote system, the incompatibility makes communication difficult.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes a virtual terminal management model where a canonical virtual terminal provides a standard representation of terminal behavior. Adaptation units translate between the physical properties of real devices and the virtual terminal's abstract interface, allowing any real device to communicate with any remote system.
tldr.outcome: Workstations can host multiple concurrent conversations (each in a logical terminal), switch between them, and adapt any device to any protocol without changing the underlying systems.

today: RFC 782 presents a forward-looking model for the early 1980s. While the specific virtual terminal management approach described was not widely adopted, the concepts of terminal abstraction, adaptation, and device independence influenced later terminal protocols and user interface design principles.

sections.title: The Virtual Terminal Abstraction
sections.content:
As personal workstations with processing power moved closer to users, the problem arose of how diverse devices could interact with remote systems. Real terminals differ in character sets, keyboard layouts, and display capabilities. The Virtual Terminal Management (VTM) model solves this by defining a canonical virtual terminal with a well-defined architecture that serves as a common language between local devices and remote systems.

The model is designed for device-independent, bi-directional, 8-bit byte-oriented communications. A Virtual Terminal Protocol uses the virtual terminal's features to provide an intermediate representation, allowing translation between site-specific codes and the virtual domain to be transparent to the communicating systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of every terminal learning every other terminal's language, they all learn one common pretend language that gateways translate to and from.

sections.title: Terminals, Adaptation Units, and Workstations
sections.content:
The VTM model has three layers. At the bottom are virtual terminals (the canonical devices), which are abstractions with no single physical realization. In the middle are adaptation units, which provide step transformation between the virtual terminal domain and the properties of real physical devices. At the top are workstations and end-users.

A single workstation can request multiple virtual terminals for concurrent conversations. Multiple workstations can share a single virtual terminal. The model defines virtual terminal classes for different behaviors: stream (continuous flow), line (line-at-a-time), logical page, physical page, and graphics. Each class has a virtual controller, virtual keys (input), and virtual display (output), plus a data store for the device state.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine the real terminal is a player and the virtual terminal is a script. The adaptation unit is the director, teaching the player how to perform the script correctly.

sections.title: Workstation Capabilities
sections.content: The model supports multiple advanced capabilities for the human-machine interface. A physical workstation display can be partitioned into multiple logical displays, each with its own workspace for a separate conversation. Input devices (keyboard, mouse, pointing device) can switch between conversations. The workstation can support different interaction modes simultaneously on different logical terminals. Multiple users can share a single logical terminal with both read and write access. Windows can provide selective viewing into a larger virtual display, with scrolling or file extension allowing viewing of past activity. The user can control output through simple keystroke commands to discard, suspend, or resume a conversation.
sections.plainLanguage: A workstation can show many conversations at once on the screen, switch which conversation gets your keystrokes, and remember what you saw in old conversations.

sections.title: Implementation and Future Work
sections.content: This RFC presents a work-in-progress design. A detailed specification of data structures and addressing functions is complete. The operations and control mechanisms are less complete. The authors note that current international interest in virtual terminal protocols has motivated publication as an example of mechanisms a virtual terminal should support, even though protocol standardization efforts may not include all extensions immediately. The design provides a framework for supporting device and processing capabilities not yet commonly available, and the model should not preclude future extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: This is one team's vision for how terminals should work. Other people are thinking about similar things, so this helps the discussion.
